title: Learning Factors in AI-Augmented Education: A Comparative Study of Middle and High School Students
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students’ perceptions of AI-mediated learning are structured across developmental stages, asking whether four learning factors—experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation—relate to one another in the same way for middle school and high school students. The authors frame the work around concerns that most prior AI-in-education research has focused on higher education, leaving K-12 understudied, especially with respect to how students evaluate AI tools and whether those evaluations vary by age.

The study was conducted in extracurricular computer science courses in Italy, where students used AI tools during programming-related activities. High school students worked with large language models such as Gemini and Claude for vibe coding and prompting, while middle school students used Teachable Machine and chatbot interaction in an introductory AI course. Data came from a 17-item questionnaire with Likert-scale and open-ended items, and the authors analyzed responses using correlation analysis, Mann-Whitney U tests, and text mining of student reflections.

Participants included 25 middle school students and 28 high school students. The main finding is that both groups reported generally positive experiences with AI, but the structure of their perceptions differed sharply: middle school students showed strong, positive intercorrelations across learning dimensions, suggesting a holistic evaluation pattern, whereas high school students showed weaker or near-zero correlations between several dimensions, indicating a more differentiated appraisal of usability, clarity, motivation, and comfort. The authors conclude that AI-supported educational design should be developmentally sensitive, emphasizing clarity and scaffolding for younger learners and more targeted support for older learners’ more critical and independent judgments.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey with correlation analysis and text mining, not an experimental or longitudinal causal design. It provides useful descriptive evidence on K-12 AI use, but credibility is limited for causal inference and relies on self-report measures from a small convenience sample.
impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests positive but modest perceived benefits of AI-supported programming activities, with no direct achievement effect sizes or outcome gains reported. Its main contribution is developmental insight into student perceptions rather than demonstrated instructional impact.

interventions.use_case: AI-mediated programming learning activities in middle and high school, including use of Gemini and Claude for vibe coding, prompting, code explanation, and chatbot-style interaction; middle school also used Teachable Machine with chatbot interaction as part of an introductory AI course.
Structured AI-related classroom learning activities in extracurricular computer science courses, where AI tools were embedded as instructional support rather than as a standalone tutor.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally positive attitudes toward the AI tools, with higher ratings for overall experience, ease of use, comfort, and motivation across both groups. However, the study is primarily correlational rather than causal; the strongest statistically significant group difference was for ease of use (Mann-Whitney U=192.00, p=0.0013), with high school students reporting greater usability (67.9% 'very much' easy) than middle school students (24.0%).
finding.measure: Likert-scale ratings of experience, ease of use, comfort, motivation, and willingness to use AI in other courses
finding.std_deviation: 0.85 overall experience SD in middle school; 0.65 in high school for Q1

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that AI-supported programming activities were associated with clearer, more differentiated student evaluations of usability, clarity, and learning support, especially in high school students. Middle school students showed strong positive coupling across dimensions (e.g., Experience-Clarity ρ=0.79; Clarity-Motivation ρ=0.60), whereas high school students showed weaker or near-zero links for several pairs (e.g., Experience-Motivation ρ=0.02; Experience-Comfort ρ=0.16), suggesting more critical appraisal and metacognitive differentiation rather than uniformly positive reactions.
finding.measure: Spearman correlations among survey dimensions and text-mined reflections on learning influence

finding.finding_summary: Students generally perceived the AI tools as helping them understand course content and support coding-related tasks. Open-ended responses emphasized learning support for middle schoolers ('learn', 'understand', 'helped') and more analytical support for high schoolers ('explanation', 'code', 'think'), but the paper does not report achievement test gains or learning performance effects.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceived learning support and text-mined reflections on AI influence on learning
